So earlier I asked about a product used to make an anaerobic denitrification filter, but it's looking like I may not need one after all unless somebody has a plausible explanation for what I'm seeing that disagrees with my conclusion. I've been cycling a new 55 gal. freshwater tank, and it's almost done, the ammonia is staying close to 0 even with adding new ammonia, and the nitrates have been going up, indicating conversion of nitrite. The nitrites are still off the scale, so I don't know exactly what they're at currently.

On Saturday, the nitrates were at 20 ppm, and yesterday they were up to 80 ppm already which would indicate a pretty good growth of bacteria eating up nitrites, and that led me to expect today's nitrate reading to be quite high. I just checked the water again today, and the nitrates are down to 5 ppm. I thought perhaps they had gone so far beyond the scale of the test kit that I got a bad reading, so I diluted a sample of tank water to 10% tank water, 90% tap water. Our tap water has no nitrates in it. Testing the diluted sample came up with a value just over 0 which is consistent with the undiluted reading, but way under what I expected it to be today. Something has clearly removed a very large amount of nitrates from the water in a 24 hour period.

My best guess on the cause is that we're also growing a colony of anaerobic bacteria that's consuming the nitrates and releasing it as dissolved nitrogen gas which will of course release to the atmosphere. I've been doing a bit more reading, and deep sand beds work in freshwater tanks to do exactly this, and to make a sloping hill on one side of the tank, I put in a lot of substrate. The substrate over about a third of the tank is over 4" in depth, and only a 3" depth is needed to support anaerobic activity. The substrate I used is like a course sand, so it has the surface area for it.

Does this seem plausible, or could there be something else at work here?

I think it's plausible, but I don't think it's very safe... at least if you get fish that dig around and manage to release some of the gas.. I mean, from what I know usually the gas is nitrogen but if it is H2S then that can be very deadly depending on how much you're feeding and all that, but even then it needs to be a specific bacteria just to produce H2S. I'm sure it wouldn't be enough to harm anyone if it got into the air, but I don't know about how much of it would get into the water itself or at all, let alone if it even was H2S and if a fish swam right into the bubble/air pocket! But I have a very vague knowledge about this sort of thing, I was taught that it was always good to keep sand aerated, but I've released bubbles from my sand every now and again with no issues. But I've also never paid as much attention to the levels in my tank as I do now! :P

If there's nothing else in your tank right now, no plants or anything that would absorb some of the nitrates, there really isn't any other way other than water changes/plants/media/chemical intervention to get the nitrates out definitely, as far as I know, then yeah I think you could have definitely got some of those bacterias in your sand that are converting the nitrates!

It sounds pretty interesting if you can get it to work safely, it'd be cool if you posted some pictures of it! What do you plan on putting in it?

Ya, if I have some anaerobic activity going on, which seems likely, the production of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is a concern. I was originally going to do this as an external filter because that leaves open the option of disconnecting the filter if H2S production starts happening, but if my bed is deep enough to support this on its own, then that's not an option. The one advantage an aquarium has though, is how easily H2S oxidizes. With sufficient dissolved oxygen in the water, H2S very quickly oxidizes and becomes harmless. H2S is also heavier than air, so it can essentially block the exchange of oxygen at the water's surface. I have 2 good sized air stones in the tank though, so even if there's a small build-up at the surface, oxygen will still get exchanged with the water, removing the H2S. Another advantage I can use is the tank lighting, high levels of light help neutralize H2S faster, and the Finnex planted+ is definitely bright enough to help with that. UV light in particular can help break down H2S, so I think I might add a UV sterilizer to the tank. It would help the tank's filtration anyway, and also provide some insurance against a release of H2S. The tank will also support a fair bit of plants which helps aerate the substrate just enough to keep the bacteria from fixing sulfer instead of nitrates, and the substrate is designed for plants which means it has a fair bit of available iron in it which also will oxidize H2S.

I'll keep you posted on what happens, and I'm definitely going to add a UV sterilizer to the tank as a safety precaution to help oxidize any released H2S faster.

I agree with you. It's clear there is some anaerobic activity, and it's not the only way to get rid of nitrates. In my limited experience, the best method of getting rid of nitrates is water changes. 10% to 25% a week with a consistent water source.

All that said, you get a completely different chemical profile with fish than you do when you are just cycling.
